summary: Requires DNS software that claims support for DNSSEC or A6 records to also support EDNS0. These features make messages larger, and without EDNS0 queries fall back to TCP, hurting latency and server load. It updates RFC 2535.

eli5.summary: Bigger answers do not fit in the small envelope DNS used to use. This says anyone using the new features must also support the bigger envelope.

questions: what is the minimum edns0 size for dnssec
why is dns limited to 512 bytes
subtitle: DNS software that supports DNSSEC or A6 records must also support EDNS0 so larger answers need not fall back to TCP.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC signatures and A6 records make DNS answers bigger than the 512-octet UDP limit, which forces slow, costly fallback to TCP.
tldr.mechanism: Servers and resolvers that claim DNSSEC or A6 support MUST support EDNS0 and advertise a minimum UDP message size (1220 octets for DNSSEC, 1024 for A6), and MUST handle fragmented UDP packets.
tldr.outcome: It is a Standards Track document that updates RFC 2535 and RFC 2874, and it has itself been updated by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

facts.label: TCP setup and tear down
facts.value: 5 packets, at least 3 extra round trips

today: RFC 3226 is a Proposed Standard. It has been updated by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035, so check those for the current DNSSEC rules. It is not marked as obsoleted.

sections.title: The 512-Octet Problem
sections.content:
RFC 1035 requires DNS messages sent over UDP to have a data payload of 512 octets or less, and most DNS software will not accept larger UDP datagrams. An answer that needs more gets a partial reply with the Truncation Bit set, and the requester usually retries over TCP. The RFC adds that how servers deliver truncated responses and how resolvers handle them varies widely.

TCP is expensive for a simple DNS exchange. A TCP connection needs 5 packets for setup and tear down, which means at least 3 round trips on top of the original UDP query. The server must also keep connection state, and many servers answer thousands of queries per second, so this causes significant overhead and delay.
sections.eli5: If a postcard is too small for your message, the post office tells you to come in and talk face to face instead. That takes much longer than just mailing it.

sections.title: What Makes Answers Bigger
sections.content:
DNSSEC adds a public key signature to each RR set. Signatures range from about 80 to 800 octets, and most fall between 80 and 200 octets. For performance and server load, security-aware servers and resolvers should get all the Answer and Authority data in one query without truncation. The DNSSEC OK bit lets a client say it wants DNSSEC records via EDNS0, but it does not remove the need for large answers. TSIG adds at least 70 octets to a message, and SIG(0) is the costlier alternative. Only one of them is attached per answer, so the growth is small but may still cause truncation.

IPv6 A6 records represent a 128-bit address with multiple records, each holding a domain name and a bit field. The name refers to a prefix that may need further A6 records in the answer, so a name with multiple A6 addresses can overflow 512 octets.

Root and TLD servers are affected too. The limit of 13 root servers exists because that is the most name servers and addresses that fit in one 512-octet answer for a SOA record. If roots advertised A6 or KEY records, the root NS answer would no longer fit, causing a large number of TCP connections. Large TLDs often have enough servers that A6 or KEY records would overflow the limit as well.
sections.eli5: Adding a signature or a long address to each answer is like adding stickers to every postcard. Soon the postcard no longer fits in its small envelope.

sections.title: UDP Versus TCP for Big Answers
sections.content:
The RFC concludes that any implementation supporting DNSSEC or A6 must be able to use DNS messages larger than 512 octets. The original 512 limit was set to reduce the chance of fragmentation. If one fragment of a UDP message is lost, the whole answer is useless and the query must be retried, whereas TCP retransmits only the lost segments.

The RFC says that early IP implementations handled fragmentation badly but all modern operating systems have overcome that, so sending fragmented messages is acceptable. The open issue is loss. On a connection with a high loss ratio, only TCP gives reliable transfer. Most links have low loss, so one round trip with a fragmented UDP packet beats setting up TCP to move a few thousand octets.

EDNS0 (RFC 2671) lets a client declare the largest UDP message it will accept. If the expected answer is between 512 octets and that maximum, the TCP overhead is avoided.
sections.eli5: If a long letter gets split into several envelopes and one is lost, you must ask again. Still, that is usually quicker than phoning and chatting for ages, so bigger letters are fine on good mail routes.

sections.title: The New Requirements
sections.content:
This is the actual change the RFC makes, adding requirements to RFC 2535 (DNSSEC) and RFC 2874 (A6):

  • All RFC 2535 compliant servers and resolvers MUST support EDNS0 and advertise a message size of at least 1220 octets, but SHOULD advertise 4000. The RFC warns this may be too low for high level servers and a successor may require more.
  • All RFC 2874 compliant servers and resolvers MUST support EDNS0 and advertise at least 1024 octets, but SHOULD advertise 2048. IPv6 datagrams should be 1024 octets unless the path MTU is known. That is smaller than the minimum IPv6 MTU, leaving room for extension headers or encapsulation.
  • All entities compliant with either RFC MUST be able to handle fragmented IPv4 and IPv6 UDP packets.
  • Hosts supporting both MUST use the larger required value in their EDNS0 advertisements.
sections.eli5: Anyone using the new secure or new address features must say, "I can read big envelopes," and must be able to put split-up letters back together.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says there are no additional security considerations beyond those in RFC 2671, which defines EDNS0. Its IANA Considerations section says only "None".

The security relevance is indirect: the document exists so that DNSSEC answers, with their signatures, can travel efficiently in a single UDP exchange instead of falling back to TCP.
sections.eli5: This note adds no new danger. It just makes sure the secure answers can be delivered quickly.
